McNab | synonyms_ref = {{Tropicos}}{{ThePlantList}} }} '''''Abies concolor''''', the '''white fir''', '''concolor fir''', or '''Colorado fir''', is a [[conifer]]ous tree in the pine family [[Pinaceae]]. This tree is native to the mountains of western North America, including the [[Sierra Nevada]] and southern [[Rocky Mountains]], and into the [[Sky island|isolated mountain ranges]] of southern [[Arizona]], [[New Mexico]], and [[Northern Mexico]]. It naturally occurs at elevations between {{Convert|900 and 3400|m|sp=us}}. It is popular as an ornamental landscaping tree and as a [[Christmas tree]]. == Description == This large evergreen conifer grows best in the central [[Sierra Nevada]] of California, where the record specimen was recorded as {{Convert|74.9|m|abbr=off|sp=us}} tall and measured {{Convert|4.6|m|abbr=on}} in [[diameter at breast height]] (dbh) in [[Yosemite National Park]].American Forestry Association. 1978. National register of big trees. American Forests 84(4):19-47 The typical size of white fir ranges from {{Convert|25–60|m|abbr=on}} tall and up to {{Convert|2.7|m|abbr=on}} dbh. The largest specimens are found in the central Sierra Nevada, where the largest diameter recorded was found in [[Sierra National Forest]] at {{Convert|58.5 x 8.5|m|abbr=on}} (1972); the west slope of the Sierra Nevada is also home to the tallest specimen on record, {{Convert|78.8|m|abbr=on}} in height.{{Cite web|last=Taylor|first=M.|title=New World Record for White Fir|url=http://ents-bbs.org/viewtopic.php?f=69&t=8774|website=Native Tree Society}} ''Abies concolor'' subsp. ''concolor'' ([[Rocky mountain]] white fir) rarely exceeds {{Convert|38|m|abbr=on}} tall or {{Convert|0.9|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=4}} dbh. Large (but not huge) trees in good soil range from {{Convert|40 to 60|m|abbr=on}} tall and from {{Convert|99 to 165|cm|sp=us}} dbh in California and southwestern Oregon and to {{Convert|41|m|abbr=on}} tall and {{Convert|124|cm|abbr=on}} dbh in [[Arizona]] and New Mexico.Jones, John R. 1974. Silviculture of southwestern mixed conifers and aspen: the status of our knowledge. USDA Forest Service, Research Paper RM-122. Rocky Mountain Forest and Range Experiment Station, Fort Collins, CO. 44 p. The dead tree tops sometimes fork into new growth. The gray bark is usually at least {{Convert|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} thick, and brown-hued inside.{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle |pages=128–135 |language=en |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}} The [[leaves]] are needle-like, flattened, {{convert|2.5|–|8|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|mm|in|frac=32|sp=us}} wide by {{convert|0.5|–|1|mm|in|frac=64|abbr=on}} thick, green to glaucous blue-green above, and with two glaucous blue-white bands of stomatal bloom below, and slightly notched to bluntly pointed at the tip. The leaf arrangement is spiral on the shoot, but with each leaf variably twisted at the base so they all lie in either two more-or-less flat ranks on either side of the shoot, or upswept across the top of the shoot but not below the shoot.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} The [[conifer cone|cones]] are {{convert|6|–|12|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|4|–|4.5|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} broad, green or purple ripening pale brown, with about 100–150 scales; the scale bracts are short, and hidden in the closed cone. The winged [[seed]]s are released when the cones disintegrate at maturity about 6 months after pollination.{{eFloras|1|233500005|Abies concolor |family=Pinaceae |first=Richard S. |last=Hunt }} White fir can live over 300 years.{{cite web |title=Plant Fact Sheet: White Fir {{hyphen}} Abies concolor |url=https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_abco.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221012807/https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_abco.pdf |archive-date=2016-12-21 |access-date=2022-03-03 |website=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]}} === Subspecies === As treated here, there are two [[subspecies]];{{cite web |title=''Abies concolor'' (white fir, abeto del Colorado) description |website=The Gymnosperm Database |date=2026-08-18 |url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Abies_concolor.php |access-date=2026-08-18}} these are also variously treated at either the lower rank of [[Variety (botany)|variety]] by some authors,{{cite web |last=Christian |first=Tom |title=''Abies concolor'' (Gordon) Lindl. ex Hildebr. |website=Trees and Shrubs Online |date=2026-08-18 |url=https://www.treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/abies/abies-concolor/ |access-date=2026-08-18}} or as distinct species by others,{{cite web |title=''Abies'' in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |website=www.efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=100024 |access-date=2026-08-18}}{{PLANTS|symbol=ABLO|taxon=Abies lowiana|access-date=14 December 2017}} or even without distinction at all.{{cite web |title=''Abies concolor'' (Gordon & Glend.) Lindl. ex Hildebr. |website=Plants of the World Online |date=2011-08-19 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:1031026-2 |access-date=2026-08-18}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! ''concolor''''' — '''Colorado white fir''' or '''Rocky Mountain white fir'''||A smaller tree to {{convert|25|–|35|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} tall, rarely {{convert|45|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}}. Foliage blue-green, strongly upcurved to erect on all except weak, shaded shoots in the lower crown; leaves mostly {{convert|3.5|–|6|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}}, and strongly glaucous on the upper side with numerous [[stoma]]ta. Tolerates winter [[temperature]]s down to about {{convert|-40|°C|°F|abbr=on}}. ||In the United States, at altitudes of {{convert|1700|–|3400|m|ft|abbr=on}} in the Rocky Mountains through Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico. and on the higher [[Great Basin]] mountains of [[Nevada]] and extreme southeastern California, and a short distance into northern [[Sonora]], Mexico. |- |[[File:Abies concolor 8065.jpg|120px]] ||'''''Abies concolor'' subsp. ''lowiana''''' ([[syn.]] ''Abies lowiana'') — '''Low's white fir''' or '''Sierra Nevada white fir''' || A larger tree growing to {{convert|40|–|60|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} tall. Foliage flattened on lower crown shoots, the leaves often raised above the shoot on upper crown shoots but not often strongly upcurved; leaves mostly {{convert|2.5|–|5|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}}, and only weakly glaucous on the upper side with few or no stomata. Tolerates winter temperatures down to about {{convert|-30|°C|°F|abbr=on}}. The United States Department of Agriculture plants database describes this subspecies as the full species '''Sierra white fir''' ''Abies lowiana'' (Gordon & Glend.) A. Murray bis. ||In the United States, at altitudes of {{convert|900|–|2300|m|ft|abbr=on}}{{eFloras|1|233500009|Abies lowiana |family=Pinaceae |first=Richard S. |last=Hunt }} from the [[Cascade Range|Cascades]] of [[Central Oregon]] south through California ([[Klamath Mountains]], Sierra Nevada) to northern Baja California, Mexico. |- |} == Botanical collection == White fir was first collected by [[Augustus Fendler]] on his expedition to the [[Santa Fe, New Mexico|Santa Fe]] area of [[New Mexico]] in 1846–1847. Fendler's patron George Engelmann, a St. Louis area physician and botanist, then described the plant.{{Cite web |last=Fendler |first=Augustus |date=2 March 1846 |title=Correspondence: Fendler (Augustus) and Engelmann (George) |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/139836 |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=Biodiversity Heritage Library}} This tree was first collected in California by [[William Lobb]] on his expedition to California of 1849–1853, after it was overlooked by [[David Douglas (botanist)|David Douglas]] in his 1825–1827 expedition to the Pacific coast region.{{cite book |last=Nisbet |first=Jack |title=David Douglas, a Naturalist at Work: An Illustrated Exploration Across Two Centuries in the Pacific Northwest |publisher=[[Sasquatch Books]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-57061-830-7 |pages=208}}Gordon, George, & Glendinning, Robert. Pinetum 155. 1858. The specific epithet ''concolor'' means "all one color", and refers to the leaves being glaucous both above and below.{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 |location=United Kingdom}} == Distribution == This tree is native to the mountains of western North America from the southern Cascade Range in [[Oregon]], south throughout [[California]] and into the [[Sierra de San Pedro Mártir]] in northern [[Baja California]], and south throughout the [[Colorado Plateau]] and southern [[Rocky Mountains]] in [[Utah]] and [[Colorado]], and into the [[Sky island|isolated mountain ranges]] of southern [[Arizona]], New Mexico, and [[Northern Mexico]]. It naturally occurs between {{Convert|900 and 3400|m|abbr=on}} above sea level. == Ecology == White fir is very closely related to [[grand fir]] (''Abies grandis''), and intergrades with it in central Oregon. It is also suggested that all of subspecies ''lowiana'' has experienced genetic introgression from grand fir.{{Cite journal |last1=Ott |first1=Todd M. |last2=Strand |first2=Eva K. |last3=Anderson |first3=Cort L. |date=2015 |title=Niche divergence of Abies grandis–Abies concolor hybrids |journal=Plant Ecology |volume=216 |issue=3 |pages=479–490 |doi=10.1007/s11258-015-0452-1 |jstor=24557678 |bibcode=2015PlEco.216..479O |issn=1385-0237}} White fir occupies a different niche than grand fir, including dryer and higher elevation sites, being more drought tolerant and having thicker, [[Fire ecology|fire-resistant]] bark. In Mexico, it is replaced by further close relatives, [[Durango fir]] (''A. durangensis'') and [[Mexican fir]] (''A. mexicana'').{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} Like grand fir, white fir is more [[shade tolerant]] than [[Douglas fir]], but less so than [[western hemlock]] and [[western redcedar]]. White fir is a [[climax species]], which means the forest has reached complex maturity in [[forest succession]] in western coniferous forests of the U.S. White fir and [[yellow pine]] ([[ponderosa pine]]/[[Jeffrey pine]]) have co-existed for millennia in old growth forests throughout their range. In the presence of logging of large diameter trees and exclusion of cleansing wildfires, young trees have become abundant over the past two centuries.{{cite web |title=Benefits of Fire |url=https://www.fire.ca.gov/communications/downloads/fact_sheets/TheBenefitsofFire.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090709034839/https://www.fire.ca.gov/communications/downloads/fact_sheets/TheBenefitsofFire.pdf |archive-date=9 July 2009 |access-date=26 January 2022 |publisher=California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection}} White fir had been regarded as a pest in the past by those in the lumber industry, but this opinion has changed. White fir is now one of the most important of all commercial softwoods according to the Western Wood Products Association.{{cite web |title=White Fir |url=https://www.spi-ind.com/product_brochures/brochure-WhiteFirFacts.pdf |access-date=26 January 2022 |website=Sierra Pacific Industries}} The white fir trait of retaining lower limbs creates an escape route for medium-to-small forest birds (such as [[spotted owl]]) from larger flying predators and provides a drip zone around the roots for collecting moisture. The retained limbs can become a [[fuel ladder]] that allows flames to climb up to the canopy. Limbing-up white fir, instead of removing medium to large diameter trees, in areas where the public is more likely to start fires can help keep other trees and specifically giant sequoia from experiencing canopy fire. Recent concern for sequoia groves has caused agencies to call for removal of white fir in the Sierra Nevada. While [[Sequoiadendron giganteum|sequoia]] seedlings and young saplings are highly susceptible to mortality or serious injury by fire; mature sequoias are fire adapted with: fire-resistant bark, elevated canopies, self-pruning lower branches, latent buds, and serotinous cones. The sequoia ecosystem is incomplete without the mixed pine/fir and oak that make up the mid and understory.{{Cite web |title=Sequoiadendron giganteum |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/seqgig/all.html |website=www.fs.fed.us}} [[Giant Sequoia]]'s cones release seeds when the heat of fire triggers them to open while the thick bark protects the inner [[cambium]] from fire damage.[https://web.archive.org/web/20121022031750/http://www.cr.nps.gov/history/online_books/science/hartesveldt/chap6.htm The Giant Sequoia of the Sierra Nevada] This tree is host to [[Phoradendron pauciflorum|fir mistletoe]] (''Phoradendron pauciflorum'') and [[Arceuthobium abietinum|fir dwarf mistletoe]] (''Arceuthobium abietinum''), two species of [[parasitic plant]].{{Cite book |last=Mathiasen |first=Robert L. |title=Mistletoes of the Continental United States and Canada |date=2021 |publisher=BRIT Press |isbn=978-1-889878-66-9 |series=Botanical miscellany |location=Fort Worth, Texas}} It is attacked by many types of insects, such as the [[Scolytus ventralis|fir engraver]] (''Scolytus ventralis'').Maloney P. E. & D. M. Rizzo. (2002). Pathogens and insects in a pristine forest ecosystem: the Sierra San Pedro Martir, Baja, Mexico. ''Canadian Journal of Forest Research'' 32:3 448-57. === Dependent species === Mature white fir–yellow pine forests support [[old-growth]] dependent wildlife species such as California [[spotted owl]] (''Strix occidentalis occidentalis''), Mount Pinos [[sooty grouse]] (''Dendragapus fuliginosus howardi''), and [[Fisher (animal)|Pacific fisher]] (''Pekania pennanti''). The spotted owl and fisher utilize cavities in [[decadent]] large-diameter white fir for nesting and denning.{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1093/jmammal/gyv083|title = Reproduction, abundance, and population growth for a fisher (Pekania pennanti) population in the Sierra National Forest, California|journal = Journal of Mammalogy|volume = 96|issue = 4|pages = 772–790|year = 2015|last1 = Sweitzer|first1 = Rick A.|last2 = Popescu|first2 = Viorel D.|last3 = Barrett|first3 = Reginald H.|last4 = Purcell|first4 = Kathryn L.|last5 = Thompson|first5 = Craig M.|doi-access = free}} The Mount Pinos sooty grouse requires large diameter trees for thermal cover and its winter diet consists of mostly white fir and yellow pine needles. This subspecies of sooty grouse has been extirpated along with a significant number of large diameter white fir from much of its range. Other subspecies of sooty grouse also utilize Douglas fir, which does not occur in the range of Mount Pinos sooty grouse.{{cite journal |last1=Bland |first1=James D. |title=Mount Pinos Sooty Grouse |journal=Studies of Western Birds |date=2008 |pages=102{{en dash}}06 |url=https://nrm.dfg.ca.gov/FileHandler.ashx?DocumentID=10383&inline |access-date=26 January 2022}} Squirrel also frequent the tree's branches.{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |page=196}} Deer browse the foliage of this species and porcupines chew the bark. Songbirds, grouse, and various mammals eat the seeds.{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |isbn=0-394-73127-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/360 360] |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/360 }} == Uses == White fir and grand fir were used by Native Americans for medicinal use involving powdered bark or pitch to treat tuberculosis or skin ailments. The [[Nlaka'pamux]] used the bark to cover lodges and make canoes. Branches were also used as bedding. White fir is a preferred construction species because of its nail-holding ability, lightness in weight, and resistance to split, twist, and pitch. It is straight-grained, non-resinous, fine-textured, stiff, and strong.Western Wood Products Association (WWPA) It is popular as a [[Christmas tree]] and for [[Christmas]] decoration owing to its soft needles, generally excellent needle retention and abundance. It is often marketed as concolor or white fir.{{Cite web|url=http://www.christmastree.org/types.cfm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116205446/http://www.christmastree.org/types.cfm|title=Christmas Tree Types|archive-date=16 January 2009|access-date=2 March 2022}} ===Cultivation=== White fir is widely planted as an [[ornamental tree]] in parks and larger [[garden]]s, particularly some [[cultivar]]s of subsp. ''concolor'' selected for very bright glaucous blue foliage, such as cv. 'Violacea'. The dwarf cultivar 'Compacta', growing to a maximum height and spread of {{convert| 2.5|m|ft|abbr=on}}, has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/93016/i-Abies-concolor-i-Compacta/Details | title = ''Abies concolor'' 'Compacta' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 14 August 2019}}{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 1 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 14 August 2019}} ==Gallery== Image:Abies_concolor_8076.jpg|''A. concolor'' subsp.
